title: Why Do We Yawn? Science Still Isn't Sure
description:
You do it about nine times a day, you started before you were born, and you can catch it from a friend. Here are the leading scientific ideas about why we yawn, and the one that didn't survive testing.

Sources:
- Frontiers in Neuroscience (2013), The thermoregulatory theory of yawning: what we know from over five years of research: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3534187/
- Cleveland Clinic, Yawning: https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/body/yawning

This video is for educational purposes only and is not medical advice.

sources.title: Frontiers in Neuroscience (2013) - The thermoregulatory theory of yawning: what we know from over five years of research

scenes.narration: You might yawn just watching this. Scientists still can't fully explain why we do it, but they do have some strong suspects.
scenes.headline: WHY DO WE YAWN?

visual.note: person mid-yawn at a work desk

scenes.narration: A yawn is a whole routine. You open your jaw wide, take a long, deep breath, pause, then breathe out. It usually lasts four to seven seconds, and the average adult yawns about nine times a day.
scenes.headline: ABOUT NINE YAWNS A DAY
scenes.sub: Each one lasts four to seven seconds

visual.spec: four-step yawn sequence: jaw opens wide, deep inhale, pause, quick exhale, with a timer showing four to seven seconds

scenes.narration: The oldest idea says yawning brings in extra oxygen. It sounds logical, but it failed the test. In a 1987 experiment, people breathed air with extra oxygen or extra carbon dioxide, and their yawning didn't change.
scenes.headline: THE OXYGEN IDEA FAILED

visual.note: researcher in a lab with breathing equipment

scenes.narration: The leading idea today is brain cooling. A deep yawn pulls in cooler air and shifts blood flow through your head, a bit like a radiator. In rats, brain temperature rose just before a yawn and dropped right after.
scenes.headline: A RADIATOR FOR YOUR BRAIN?

visual.note: illustration of blood vessels supplying the brain

scenes.narration: There's support in people, too. In Tucson, Arizona, pedestrians were nearly twice as likely to yawn in winter as on scorching summer days, when the outside air was about as warm as their bodies and couldn't cool much.
scenes.headline: MORE YAWNS IN WINTER
scenes.sub: When the air can cool you

visual.note: pedestrians on a cool, sunny city street

scenes.narration: Then there's the strangest part. Yawns are contagious. Seeing or hearing someone yawn can set you off, and you're more likely to catch one from family and friends than from strangers. Many researchers link this to empathy.
scenes.headline: YAWNS ARE CONTAGIOUS

visual.note: two friends yawning at the same time

scenes.narration: And yawning starts before you're even born. Babies yawn in the womb about three months into pregnancy. That's one reason the oxygen idea never quite fit: those babies aren't breathing air at all.
scenes.headline: YAWNING BEFORE BIRTH

visual.note: gentle ultrasound image of a fetus

scenes.narration: So why do we yawn? Probably for more than one reason: cooling the brain, nudging it awake, maybe keeping a group in sync. The honest answer is that science is still working on it.
scenes.headline: THE ANSWER IS STILL OPEN

scenes.narration: Follow Inside Your Body for more of the science of you.
